connection: Production contains Employee, Address, and ClockEntry from Sessions 06–07. ScratchPad already references Domain and retains Sessions 03–05. Add a preserved ScratchPad experiment that observes value copying and reference sharing through the production models.
objectives: Predict, before running any code, whether assigning one Employee variable to another copies the object or shares it.
Assign Employee.Name through one alias to observe that two variables referring to the same Employee see the same mutation.
Explain why ClockEntry.EmployeeId (an int) and ClockIn (a DateTime) are copied by value when a ClockEntry itself is passed around, even though ClockEntry is a class.
Distinguish 'the ClockEntry reference was copied' from 'the ClockEntry's field values were copied' -- they are not the same claim.

visuals.title: Two names, one Employee
visuals.explanation: Employee employee = new(1, "Avery", address); Employee alias = employee; -- both variables hold the same reference, not two separate objects.

visuals.title: A mutation through one name is visible through the other
visuals.explanation: Assigning alias.Name changes the object both variables point to -- employee.Name reads the new value too.

visuals.title: int and DateTime are copied, always
visuals.explanation: ClockEntry.EmployeeId and ClockIn are value types -- assigning them to a new variable, or passing them as arguments, copies the number/date itself.

visuals.title: The object vs. its fields are separate questions
visuals.explanation: ClockEntry itself is a reference type (its identity can be shared); its EmployeeId and ClockIn fields are value types (their contents are always copied).

preQuiz.prompt: After Employee alias = employee; alias.Name = "Avery Nguyen";, what does employee.Name return?
options: "Nguyen" -- employee and alias refer to the same Employee object
The original name -- alias is an independent copy
A compile error -- properties cannot be assigned through an alias
preQuiz.explanation: Assigning employee to alias copies the reference, not the object -- both variables point at one Employee, so assigning Name through alias is visible through either name.

preQuiz.prompt: If you pass a ClockEntry to a method and that method reads entry.EmployeeId into a local int, then changes the local int, does the original ClockEntry.EmployeeId change?
options: No -- EmployeeId is an int (value type); reading it into a local variable copies the number, and EmployeeId itself has no public setter anyway
Yes -- ClockEntry is a class, so everything about it is shared
It depends on whether the method is static
preQuiz.explanation: EmployeeId's value is copied into the local int the moment it is read; the two are independent from that point on, and ClockEntry.EmployeeId is get-only regardless.

preQuiz.prompt: Is ClockEntry a reference type or a value type?
options: Reference type -- it is declared with class, so assigning a ClockEntry variable copies the reference, not a new object
Value type -- it holds only an int and two DateTimes
Both, depending on how it is constructed
preQuiz.explanation: class always means reference type in C#, regardless of what value-type fields the class happens to contain.

concept.title: Assigning a class variable copies the reference
paragraphs: Employee alias = employee copies the reference stored in employee -- a pointer to one Employee object in memory -- into alias. It does not create a second Employee.
Assigning Name through alias changes the same object employee refers to, because there was only ever one object.

concept.title: Assigning a value-type field copies the value
paragraphs: ClockEntry.EmployeeId and ClockIn are int and DateTime -- value types. Reading either one into a local variable copies the number or date; the local variable has no ongoing connection to the ClockEntry it came from.
This is true even though ClockEntry the class is a reference type -- the type of the whole object and the type of each of its members are separate questions.

concept.title: Passing an object as a method argument passes its reference
paragraphs: ClockEntryService.ClockIn constructs a ClockEntry and passes it directly to SaveClockEntry -- the repository receives the same object, not a copy, and adds that exact reference to _clockEntries.

This is why ClockEntryService.Clockout can retrieve that same ClockEntry later via GetClockEntry and call ClockOutEmployee on it -- it is mutating the one object that has existed since ClockIn, not a disconnected copy.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can ClockEntryService.Clockout mutate the same ClockEntry that ClockIn created, days apart in the method call sequence?
options: ClockIn passed the object's reference to SaveClockEntry, so the repository has held the one real object the whole time -- GetClockEntry hands that same reference back out
ClockEntry overrides Equals to look up entries by value
ClockOutEmployee creates a brand new ClockEntry internally
postQuiz.explanation: There is exactly one ClockEntry object per clock-in; every method that touches it afterward is operating on that same shared reference.

postQuiz.prompt: If Employee.Address were reassigned with new Address("456 Oak Street", "Riverton") through one alias, what would a second alias see?
options: The new Address -- Address itself is also a reference-type property being reassigned on the one shared Employee object
The old Address -- Address is a value type
postQuiz.explanation: Address is assigned to Employee's Address property, and Employee itself is shared -- so any alias reading employee.Address afterward sees the newly assigned reference.

postQuiz.prompt: Does calling entry.GetDuration() copy the ClockEntry?
options: No -- entry is passed implicitly as the reference this method call operates on; no copy of the object occurs
Yes -- every method call copies its receiver
postQuiz.explanation: Method calls on a reference-type instance operate on the shared object directly, not on a copy.

reflections.question: Why does assigning Employee.Name through one alias matter for anything other than this one lesson -- where else in the app could that behavior be observed?
reflections.answer: Any code that stores or passes the same Employee reference can observe in-place property mutation through that reference. For example, an Employee kept in EmployeeDirectory remains the same object after Name changes, so later lookups observe the new value without replacing the dictionary entry. The same reasoning applies whenever a service, collection, or caller shares that Employee object.

reflections.question: What would you have to change about ClockEntry for two separately-constructed ClockEntry objects with the same EmployeeId and ClockIn to be considered 'equal'?
reflections.answer: ClockEntry would need value-equality behavior, such as overriding Equals and GetHashCode and usually the == and != operators, or being redesigned as a record. The equality definition would also need to decide whether ClockOut participates. That choice is consequential because collections could then treat two distinct clock-entry events with matching values as one item.

reflections.question: How does knowing SaveClockEntry stores a live reference (not a copy) change how you would reason about a bug where an entry's ClockOut value seems to change unexpectedly?
reflections.answer: Trace every alias to that ClockEntry instead of assuming the repository owns an isolated copy. A caller that still holds the original reference, or code that retrieves the same reference, can mutate the object seen by the repository. If isolation were required, the design would need copying, immutability, or a narrower mutation boundary.

whatBreaks: Assuming Employee assignment copies the object would lead you to expect assigning alias.Name to leave employee.Name unchanged -- it does not, and code relying on that wrong assumption would silently read stale names. Assuming ClockEntry.EmployeeId is somehow 'live' after being copied into a local variable would lead to bugs trying to use that local as if it still tracked the entry. Forgetting that SaveClockEntry holds a live reference (not a defensive copy) means any code that later mutates a ClockEntry object directly is also mutating what the repository has stored.
summary: Employee is a reference type: assigning it copies the reference, so changing Name through one alias is visible through every other alias. ClockEntry's EmployeeId and ClockIn are value types: copying them copies the number or date itself, independent of ClockEntry's own reference-type identity. SaveClockEntry stores the exact reference ClockIn constructs -- the mechanism that lets Clockout later mutate the same object.
